lessons.title: Roller Milling for Flakes
lessons.body:
Roller milling is the heart of flake production. You need a roller mill with two smooth steel rollers, each about 20-30 cm in diameter and 30-50 cm long. The rollers spin at different speeds: the front roller turns faster than the back roller. This difference in speed creates a shearing action that flattens grain into flakes. For maize, millet, or sorghum, you first clean the grain and remove stones. Then you temper it by adding water to reach 16-20% moisture. Let it rest for 4-8 hours in a sealed container. This softens the grain so it flattens without cracking.

Set the gap between rollers to about 0.5 mm for thin flakes, or 1 mm for thicker ones. Feed grain into the hopper slowly and evenly. Too fast and the rollers jam; too slow and you get uneven flakes. The rollers must be perfectly parallel. Check with a feeler gauge. If one side is tighter, flakes will be thicker on that side. After rolling, you get wet flakes that stick together. Break them apart gently by hand or with a rotating breaker bar.

In Africa, many small producers use locally made roller mills from Kenya or Nigeria. These cost between $500 and $2,000. They run on a 2-5 HP electric motor or a diesel engine. A good mill can process 50-100 kg per hour. Clean the rollers after each use with a stiff brush and dry cloth. Never use water on the rollersâit causes rust. Apply a thin film of food-grade oil weekly. If flakes come out torn or powdery, the grain is too dry or the roller gap is too wide. Adjust moisture or gap. With practice, you will produce consistent flakes that toast evenly and taste great.

lessons.title: Flaking Process: Tempering, Rolling, and Toasting
lessons.body:
Tempering is the first critical step. For maize, add 1.5 liters of clean water to 10 kg of grain in a plastic drum. Mix well and seal for 6 hours. For sorghum, use 1.2 liters per 10 kg and rest for 4 hours. The goal is 18% moisture. Test by biting a grain: it should be soft but not mushy. If too dry, add a little more water and wait another hour. If too wet, spread on a mat for 30 minutes.

Rolling comes next. Set your roller mill gap to 0.4-0.6 mm. Feed tempered grain at a steady rate. Catch the flakes on a clean tray. They should be about 1 mm thick and flexible, not brittle. If they crumble, the grain is too dry. If they stick to the rollers, it's too wet. Adjust accordingly. Work in small batches of 5 kg so you can control quality.

Toasting dries and browns the flakes. Use a hot air oven, a drum roaster, or a solar dryer. For oven toasting, spread flakes in a single layer on a baking tray. Toast at 150Â°C for 10-12 minutes. Turn once at 6 minutes. They are done when they are golden brown and crisp. For drum roasting, heat the drum to 180Â°C and roast 2 kg of flakes for 5-7 minutes, stirring constantly. Solar drying takes 4-6 hours on a clear day. After toasting, cool flakes on a wire rack. They should snap when broken. Pack in airtight containers. In humid African climates, add a desiccant sachet to keep them crunchy. Properly toasted flakes last 3-6 months.

lessons.title: Granulation: Crushing and Sizing
lessons.body:
Granulation turns flakes or grains into uniform pieces for cereals like granola or instant porridge. You need a crusherâeither a hammer mill or a roller crusher. A hammer mill uses swinging hammers to smash grain against a screen. A roller crusher passes grain between two corrugated rollers. For small-scale production, a hammer mill with a 2 mm screen is ideal. It costs $300-$800 and runs on a 3 HP motor. Feed dry grain or toasted flakes into the hopper. The hammers break them into smaller pieces. The screen size controls the final particle size: 2 mm for coarse granules, 1 mm for finer.

After crushing, you must size the granules. Use a set of sieves with mesh sizes 2 mm, 1 mm, and 0.5 mm. Stack them from coarse on top to fine at bottom. Shake by hand or use a mechanical shaker for 2-3 minutes. The granules that stay on the 2 mm sieve are too largeâcrush them again. The ones on the 1 mm sieve are your standard granules. The ones on 0.5 mm are fine granules. The dust that passes through is flour; you can sell it as porridge flour or add it back to the crusher with a little water to form larger granules.

In Africa, granulation is key for making instant maize porridge or millet granules. For a typical batch, crush 10 kg of toasted flakes. You will get about 7 kg of usable granules, 2 kg of flour, and 1 kg of oversize that you re-crush. Always wear a dust mask when crushingâflour dust can harm your lungs. Clean the crusher after each use. Replace worn hammers or screens every 200-300 hours of operation. Store granules in airtight bags away from moisture. They keep for 6 months.

lessons.title: Production of Granola and Muesli
lessons.body:
Granola and muesli are ready-to-eat cereals made from rolled oats, nuts, seeds, and dried fruit. In Africa, you can use local ingredients: rolled oats (imported or locally milled), crushed groundnuts, sesame seeds, sunflower seeds, dried mango, banana chips, and honey or brown sugar. A basic granola recipe: mix 5 kg rolled oats, 1 kg crushed groundnuts, 0.5 kg sesame seeds, and 0.5 kg sunflower seeds in a large bowl. In a separate pot, warm 1 kg honey and 0.5 kg vegetable oil. Pour over the dry mix and stir until everything is coated. Spread on baking trays and bake at 160Â°C for 20-25 minutes, stirring every 8 minutes. The granola is done when golden and dry. Add 1 kg chopped dried fruit after bakingâthis prevents burning. Cool completely before packing.

For muesli, you do not bake. Mix 5 kg rolled oats, 1 kg raisins or dried fruit, 0.5 kg crushed nuts, and 0.5 kg seeds. Add 0.2 kg brown sugar if you like it sweeter. Stir well. Pack in airtight bags or jars. Muesli is softer and chewier than granola. Both are high in fiber and energy. In many African cities, granola sells for $5-$10 per kg in supermarkets. You can produce 10 kg per day with a single oven and two workers.

Key points: use clean, dry equipment. Keep nuts and seeds freshârancid nuts ruin the taste. For longer shelf life, toast nuts and seeds before mixing. Store in a cool, dry place. Label with production date and best-before date (6 months for granola, 4 months for muesli). You can also add local flavors like baobab powder, moringa, or cinnamon. Start small, test your product with neighbors, and adjust sweetness and crunch to local taste.

lessons.title: Quality Control in Flake Production
lessons.body:
Quality control starts with raw materials. Buy clean grain with less than 2% foreign matter. Test moisture with a moisture meter (cost $50-$150) or by the salt method: mix 10 g of ground grain with 20 g of dry salt in a sealed jar. Shake for 1 minute. If salt sticks to the jar, grain is too wet (above 16%). If it flows freely, moisture is good. For flaking, you need 16-20% moisture. Too dry gives broken flakes; too wet gives sticky, clumped flakes.

During rolling, check flake thickness every 15 minutes with a micrometer or caliper. Target 0.8-1.2 mm. If thickness varies by more than 0.2 mm, adjust roller gap. Check flake integrity: take a handful and shake. Less than 5% should break into pieces. If more, your grain is too dry or rollers are worn. After toasting, check color: golden brown, not dark brown or pale. Taste: nutty and crisp, not burnt or raw. Moisture after toasting must be below 5%. Test by weighing 10 g of flakes, drying in an oven at 105Â°C for 2 hours, and reweighing. Loss should be less than 0.5 g.

Packaging quality matters. Use food-grade polyethylene bags or lined paper bags. Seal with a heat sealer or tie tightly. Label with product name, weight, production date, and expiry date. Store in a dry room below 25Â°C and 60% humidity. Inspect every batch for insects, mold, or off-smells. Keep a sample of each batch for 1 month. If a customer complains, you can trace the problem. Train your workers to wash hands, wear clean aprons, and never smoke or eat near production. A simple quality log book helps you track moisture, thickness, and toasting time. Consistent quality builds trust and repeat sales.

lessons.title: Equipment Maintenance and Safety
lessons.body:
Your roller mill, crusher, oven, and sieves need regular care. Every day after production, brush off all flour and grain dust. Use a stiff brush and a vacuum if available. Never use water on electrical parts. For the roller mill, check the roller gap with a feeler gauge weekly. If rollers are worn unevenly, they must be reground or replaced. A machine shop can regrind them for $50-$100. Lubricate bearings every 50 hours with food-grade grease. Check belts and chains for tensionâloose belts slip and cause uneven flakes. Replace worn hammers in the crusher every 200-300 hours. Keep spare screens and hammers on hand.

Safety is non-negotiable. Roller mills and crushers have rotating parts that can crush fingers. Always turn off and unplug the machine before cleaning or adjusting. Never put your hand into the hopper while it is running. Use a wooden pusher to feed grain. Wear tight-fitting clothes, no loose sleeves or jewelry. Tie back long hair. Wear safety glasses when using a hammer millâflying particles can blind you. Wear ear protection if the machine is loud. Keep a first aid kit nearby. In case of a cut, stop bleeding and seek medical help.

Fire safety: flour dust is flammable. Keep the work area clean and free of dust clouds. Do not smoke. Install a fire extinguisher (dry powder type) near the production area. Electrical safety: use proper wiring and earthing. Do not overload sockets. If you smell burning, turn off the main switch. For ovens, use gloves when loading and unloading trays. Keep children away from all machines. Train every worker on safe operation before they touch any equipment. A safe workplace is a productive workplace.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Flaking & Granulation in African Breakfast Cereal Production

This practical reference is designed for African cereal processors â from small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa, and Zambia to larger millers â who want to move from raw grain to shelf-ready flakes and granola. It focuses on the business case: yield, throughput, cost per kilogram, product consistency, and compliance with regional food safety standards. The module assumes you already understand the basics of roller milling, tempering, rolling, toasting, crushing, and sizing. Here we translate theory into operational decisions you can make on the factory floor.

Why Flaking and Granulation Matter for African Agribusiness

Breakfast cereals are one of the fastest-growing food categories in sub-Saharan Africa, driven by urbanization, rising incomes, and demand for convenient, shelf-stable foods. Flaking and granulation are the core unit operations that convert inexpensive grains â maize, sorghum, millet, oats, and rice â into higher-value products. For a processor, the difference between a profitable operation and a marginal one often comes down to three things: yield (how much saleable product you get per tonne of grain), consistency (flake thickness, color, texture), and throughput (tonnes per hour). This reference gives you the practical numbers and checks to manage all three.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Roller Milling and Toasting

Roller mills and toasting ovens are high-risk equipment. Never reach into the nip point of rollers while the machine is running â even at low speed, rollers can crush fingers and hands. Always use lockout/tagout (LOTO) procedures before clearing jams or adjusting roll gaps. Toasting ovens operate at 150â180Â°C; use heat-resistant gloves and face shields when loading or unloading. Ensure adequate ventilation to prevent dust explosions â cereal dust is combustible. In African SME settings, ensure at least one trained first-aider is present and that fire extinguishers (dry powder or COâ) are within 10 metres of milling and toasting areas. Comply with national occupational safety regulations (e.g., Kenya's OSHA 2007, Nigeria's Factories Act).

Practical Business Considerations for African Processors

Yield optimization: A 1% improvement in flake yield on a 500 kg/h line can add 5 kg/h of saleable product â over a 2,000-hour year, that's 10 tonnes of extra product. At $1.50/kg, that's $15,000 in additional revenue. Small adjustments to tempering time and roll gap often deliver this.

Energy costs: Toasting and drying are the most energy-intensive steps. In many African countries, electricity and fuel costs are high and unreliable. Consider solar-assisted drying or biomass-powered toasters where feasible. A well-controlled toasting step also reduces rework and waste.

Local grain sourcing: Using locally available grains (sorghum, millet, maize) reduces raw material costs and supports local farmers. However, local grains vary in moisture, hardness, and starch properties. You must adjust tempering and roll gaps accordingly. Build relationships with suppliers and test each batch.

Packaging and shelf life: Flakes are hygroscopic. In humid African climates, packaging must be a high moisture barrier (e.g., metallized film or high-density polyethylene with desiccant). Target aw <0.6 and moisture <5% to achieve 6â12 months shelf life without preservatives.

Regulatory compliance: Exporting to regional markets (e.g., ECOWAS, EAC) requires compliance with Codex Alimentarius and national standards. Keep records of moisture, aw, and foreign matter tests. This is not just bureaucracy â it's a competitive advantage when bidding for supermarket contracts.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Grain intake: Verify moisture content (<14% for storage) and foreign matter (<1%) before processing.
  • Tempering: Target 18â22% moisture for maize/sorghum; allow 4â12 hours for uniform hydration.
  • Roll gap: Check and adjust before each production run; use feeler gauges and record settings.
  • Toasting: Monitor temperature and time; aim for golden color and moisture <5%.
  • Granulation: Use sieves to ensure particle size 2â6 mm for granola; reject fines and oversize.
  • Quality control: Test moisture, aw, thickness, and color every 2 hours; log results.
  • Safety: Enforce LOTO, wear PPE, and keep fire extinguishers accessible.
  • Packaging: Use moisture-barrier film; seal immediately after filling; label with production date and best-before.

Further Reading

  • FAO (1995) â Sorghum and Millets in Human Nutrition â free full text on grain processing, including flaking and granulation.
  • FAO (2001) â Principles and Practices of Small- and Medium-Scale Cereal Processing â practical guidance for African SMEs.
  • Codex Alimentarius (2007) â Code of Hygienic Practice for Cereals â international food safety standard.
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) â national standards for cereal products (search for relevant standards).
  • African Cereals Network â regional resources and research on cereal processing (check for free publications).

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for grain before flaking?
quiz.explanation: Tempering grain to 16-20% moisture softens it for proper flaking without cracking.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of tempering grain before rolling?
options: B) To soften the grain for even flaking
quiz.explanation: Tempering adds moisture to soften the grain so it flattens without breaking.

quiz.q: How long should you rest maize after adding water for tempering?
quiz.explanation: Maize needs about 6 hours of resting for moisture to penetrate evenly.

quiz.q: What gap setting is recommended for thin flakes?
quiz.explanation: A 0.5 mm gap produces thin flakes, while 1 mm gives thicker flakes.

quiz.q: Why should you never use water to clean roller mill rollers?
quiz.explanation: Water causes steel rollers to rust, damaging the surface and affecting flake quality.

quiz.q: What temperature is recommended for oven toasting flakes?
quiz.explanation: Toasting at 150Â°C for 10-12 minutes gives golden, crisp flakes without burning.

quiz.q: How can you tell if toasted flakes are properly dried?
quiz.explanation: Properly toasted flakes are crisp and snap when broken, indicating low moisture.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a hammer mill in granulation?
options: B) To crush grain into smaller pieces
quiz.explanation: A hammer mill uses swinging hammers to smash grain against a screen, creating granules.

quiz.q: What screen size is ideal for coarse granules?
quiz.explanation: A 2 mm screen produces coarse granules, while 1 mm gives finer granules.

quiz.q: After crushing, what should you do with granules larger than 2 mm?
quiz.explanation: Oversize granules are re-crushed to achieve uniform particle size.

quiz.q: What is the typical yield of usable granules from 10 kg of toasted flakes?
quiz.explanation: About 70% becomes usable granules, with the rest as flour and oversize.

quiz.q: Why should you wear a dust mask during crushing?
options: B) To protect lungs from flour dust
quiz.explanation: Flour dust can harm lungs, so a dust mask is essential for safety.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between granola and muesli?
options: A) Granola is baked, muesli is not
B) Muesli is baked, granola is not
quiz.explanation: Granola is baked with honey and oil, while muesli is a raw mixture of oats, nuts, and dried fruit.

quiz.q: At what temperature should granola be baked?
quiz.explanation: Baking at 160Â°C for 20-25 minutes gives golden, crunchy granola.

quiz.q: When should dried fruit be added to granola?
quiz.explanation: Adding dried fruit after baking prevents burning and keeps it chewy.

quiz.q: How long does properly stored granola last?
quiz.explanation: Granola stored in airtight containers in a cool, dry place lasts about 6 months.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to test grain moisture without a meter?
quiz.explanation: The salt method uses dry salt and a jar to estimate moisture by clumping.

quiz.q: What is the target flake thickness for quality control?
quiz.explanation: Flakes should be 0.8-1.2 mm thick for consistent toasting and texture.

quiz.q: What should the moisture content be after toasting flakes?
quiz.explanation: Toasted flakes must be below 5% moisture to stay crisp and prevent mold.

quiz.q: Why keep a sample of each batch for one month?
options: B) For traceability if complaints arise
quiz.explanation: Samples help trace quality issues if a customer complains.

quiz.q: How often should you check roller gap with a feeler gauge?
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks ensure rollers remain parallel and flake thickness is consistent.

quiz.q: What type of grease should be used on roller mill bearings?
quiz.explanation: Food-grade grease is safe for equipment that contacts food.

quiz.q: What should you do before cleaning a roller mill?
quiz.explanation: Always unplug equipment before cleaning to prevent accidental injury.

quiz.q: Why is flour dust dangerous?
quiz.explanation: Flour dust can ignite and cause explosions if concentrated in the air.

quiz.q: What should you use to push grain into a running mill?
quiz.explanation: A wooden pusher keeps hands safe from rotating rollers.

quiz.q: How often should crusher hammers be replaced?
quiz.explanation: Worn hammers reduce efficiency and should be replaced every 200-300 hours.

quiz.q: What is a sign that grain is too dry for flaking?
quiz.explanation: Too dry grain produces brittle flakes that crumble instead of flattening.

quiz.q: What local ingredient can add African flavor to granola?
quiz.explanation: Baobab powder is a local African ingredient that adds tangy flavor and nutrients.

quiz.q: What is the recommended storage humidity for flakes?
quiz.explanation: Low humidity below 60% prevents flakes from absorbing moisture and losing crunch.

quiz.q: What should you do if you smell burning from an electrical machine?
quiz.explanation: Turning off the main switch prevents electrical fire or damage.
